• Name: Ghost shrimp (Glass shrimp, Grass shrimp)
  • Scientific name: Palaemonetes paludosus
  • Optimal tank size: 10 gallons (~40 litres)
  • Breeding: medium to difficult
  • Optimal KH: 5–8 (3–12)
  • TDS (optimal): 150–200 (100–400)
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: algae eater/omnivore
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Colour form: transparent, orange, yellow

Biologists once believed that Ghost shrimp belonged to the Caridina genus. This was later revised, and they do not even share the same family.

"Ghost shrimp" is a collective name covering many species of the genus Palaemonetes, and often Macrobrachium species too, so there is a lot of confusion. Similar-looking shrimp include Palaemonetes sinensis (Far Eastern freshwater shrimp), Palaemonetes varians (Atlantic ditch shrimp), Palaemonetes argentinus (Argentinean shrimp), Palaemonetes antennarius (Popcorn shrimp) and Palaemonetes kadiakensis (Mississippi grass shrimp). Instead of the American ghost shrimp you may receive Macrobrachium species such as Macrobrachium ehemals (Indian ghost shrimp) or Macrobrachium lanchesteri (Whisker shrimp), freshwater river shrimp or even some brackish water forms. Macrobrachium lanchesteri is much more aggressive and can hunt dwarf shrimp (such as adult red cherry shrimp), small fish and snails.

Macrobrachium ghost shrimp (Whisker shrimp)American ghost shrimp (normal ghost shrimp)
Longer front legs, larger front claws (almost as long as the body)Claws much smaller
Many develop a darker colour; 2 small red dots on the tailDo not have the red colour
Red to orange bands on the legs and feelersNo such bands
Often develop faint patterning like vertical barsUsually no body markings
Larger (~7.5 cm)Smaller (~5–6 cm)

The death rate of ghost shrimp is often high because they are usually treated as fish food and are captured and kept in poor conditions at big pet stores, under constant stress and without proper food. That stress eventually kills them even if they are later cared for well.

When buying, look at colour and activity. Healthy shrimp are almost transparent and very active. A milky colour and lethargic behaviour mean unsuitable water conditions and/or transport, so be ready for a quick die-off of some or all of them. Practice shows that if you buy 10–20, at least 4–10 survive. Any shrimp should be acclimated before being put in the tank.
Originally found in North America. Besides being popular in the shrimp hobby, they are also sold as cheap food for larger fish.

In the wild, ghost shrimp live mostly in freshwater, although they are sometimes found in slightly brackish water. Because of predators they prefer a nocturnal lifestyle. In nature they can build burrows to feed, using the claws of the first and second pairs of legs to dig and their legs to draw the sandy mud backward; these burrows are not permanent.

Females can sometimes grow up to 60 mm, so small aquariums (less than 5 gallons, 20 litres) are not suitable. Optimal tank size is about 40 litres. 1–3 ghost shrimp per gallon is an optimal number if there is nothing else in the aquarium. Do not overstock: it stresses the shrimp and makes them aggressive.

A setup similar to a cherry shrimp tank is fine. Provide basic shelter and plants. They do well in both soft and hard water and also feel fine in water that differs from the optimal parameters. Stability of water parameters can matter even more than making them optimal. Sand or small gravel can make them happier.

Growth to maturity (20 mm) takes about 2–3 months when the water temperature exceeds 26°C, and 4–5 months when it is lower.

Ghost shrimp can live up to 3 years in an aquarium under good conditions.

If they turn opaque before moulting, that is normal, but it will not be white. If they turn opaque and do not move, the moult was unsuccessful and the shrimp is stuck in its exoskeleton. If they stay white or pink for some time, they are most likely sick and usually die; it is a reaction to stress, so check water parameters and look for possible predators such as dragonfly nymphs.

Temperature 20–27°C, KH 3–12, pH 6.5–8.0 (optimal 7.0–7.4), GH 5–8 (3–15), TDS 150–200 (100–400), nitrate less than 20 ppm.

Ghost shrimp do not need brackish water to live or breed; they are predominantly a freshwater species. In laboratory experiments adults survived at a salinity of 30 ppt. Egg hatching and larval development proceed similarly at 5 ppt and 0 ppt, but at 10–20 ppt the survival rate of the eggs drops significantly. Larvae tolerate salinity as well as adults and could even metamorphose at up to 30 ppt.

Ghost shrimp are not picky eaters. In the tank they eat everything they find on the bottom, algae, tender plant leaves, leftover fish food and detritus (dead leaves, waste). They are decent scavengers and go after all shrimp or fish foods placed in the tank.

A study of around 300 stomachs found that the food of grass shrimp consisted primarily of algae, vascular plants, detritus and aquatic insects. Algae was the major food item, comprising 47% of food ingested and occurring in 83% of stomachs; insects contributed least, 15.2% of food ingested, occurring in 36.2% of stomachs. They are no match for Amano shrimp, but they do eat algae.

Calcium plays a big role for shrimp. If they start picking at live plants, it indicates they do not have enough food; they will not eat plants unless really hungry.

Ghost shrimp are bold and not shy: they crawl around the whole aquarium searching for food and do not hide during the day like most other shrimp. In the absence of big predatory fish they do not stay hidden, and they ignore fish of their size. Like most crustaceans they tend to be nocturnal scavengers.

They are usually non-aggressive, but some become a bit aggressive. They are opportunistic and can eat baby shrimp of any species or even fish fry. They are very aggressive towards each other during feeding. They can be territorial if the tank is too small and overstocked. Their claws are very small and not meant for hunting, but they can catch and eat a sick or dying animal, including snails that cannot seal themselves in their shells.

Do not keep them with any fish that can fit a shrimp in its mouth. Ideally keep them in a species-only tank, though a peaceful community also works. It is better to keep them with similar-sized or bigger species such as Amano shrimp, Malawa shrimp, Vampire shrimp or Bamboo shrimp.

Young shrimp are hard to sex; adults are easier to distinguish.

  1. Females have a greenish saddle on the back that runs along the underside of the belly; males do not. Eggs under the belly also look like glowing green dots.
  2. Females have a pronounced curved arc along the top end of the tail.
  3. Females are much larger and thicker in the abdomen. Adult females are usually 5 cm, while males are less than 4 cm. In one study, males made up only 6.7% of shrimp larger than 30 mm.

Ghost shrimp usually have no body markings, so the usual methods of sexing shrimp work only up to a point. The ideal sex ratio is 1:1, unlike other shrimp.

Breeding is almost the same as with any dwarf shrimp. When the female is ready, she moults; her pheromones then make the males search for her. The eggs are fertilised and held under her abdomen, where they develop. No special conditions are needed, and they can breed in one aquarium. Adults can eat larvae or small shrimplets, so a second tank is advisable; otherwise provide lots of plants and small hiding places. Females with eggs should be moved to a separate tank.

Female fecundity ranges from 8–85 eggs and increases with the female's length; average brood size is 35.9 eggs. Incubation in the laboratory was 12–14 days at 26–28°C. Immature females are 12–19 mm long; no females under 20 mm carried eggs. If the eggs are nearly at the bottom of the swimmeret, they will fall off soon.

The larval rearing tank can be without any filtration if it has lots of plants, since the bioload is almost zero. A very slow air stone helps distribute greenwater; water movement must be very gentle or the larvae get blown around. If a filter is used, cover the intake with a sponge or a piece of nylon stocking.

The eggs hatch as free-floating larvae, not miniature shrimp, and are too small to catch, so move the female while she still carries eggs and put her back in the main tank after the young appear. Larvae hang under the surface for a few days. They need powdered food (Spirulina is good), infusoria, artemia and zooplankton, mixed thoroughly with water; feed twice a day about 50–100 ml, using a syringe. They metamorphose into miniature adults in about 5–10 days depending on temperature; big black eyes and sharply bent backs are the most obvious features at this stage. After that they need no special care and moult frequently. Do small water changes of 5–10% every 10–14 days. Larvae in one study were reared at room temperatures varying from 15–31°C.

  1. First zoea stage: larvae 3.7–3.9 mm, straight rostrum with a dorsal hump near its base, usually without spines; yellowish with orange-red pigments; moults within about 24 hours.
  2. Second zoea stage: 3.8–4.1 mm; the eyes separate from the carapace and the last 3 pairs of pereiopods appear; the rostrum has a single dorsal spine; moults after about 2 days.
  3. Third zoea stage: 3.8–4.4 mm; uropods appear and the rostrum gains a second dorsal spine; lasts 1–4 days depending on temperature, most often moulting after 2 days.

Ghost shrimp have a semi-transparent body; depending on diet they may become yellow, orange, beige or light brown. Pigment granules let them camouflage against the background. They have a well-developed rostrum with small teeth along the dorsal and ventral surfaces, and no claws on the third pair of walking legs. The first 4 pairs of legs have tiny claws used to collect food from the substrate. They are rarely larger than 5 cm.

Many people find that they have more "personality" than Neocaridina and Caridina shrimp.
